tier_reason: First-party README and BENCHMARKS.md tables with public scripts (test/bench.sh, test/bench.c, test/gen.py) and gcc -O2 stated for the microbenchmark, but the CPU is only 'Intel Core' under WSL2 and the xsv version/build is unstated, so not A; the 76x count gain with unstated baseline build is also capped at C.

corrections.baseline: xsv (BurntSushi's Rust CSV toolkit, version and build unstated) for the command-level table; naive scalar C loops (byte count, byte find, comma walk) built with gcc -O2 in test/bench.c for the SIMD microbenchmark, not glibc memchr or an -O3 build
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Release build per Makefile: NASM -f elf64 -O2 for the assembly, gcc -O2 -DNDEBUG for the C argument parser; microbenchmark C reference built with gcc -O2 (BENCHMARKS.md, test/bench.c); gcc version and xsv build not stated
corrections.hardware: WSL2, Intel Core (model not stated), DDR4-3200
corrections.claimed_speedup: 1 GB CSV (6.27M rows, 18 columns), oxsv vs xsv: count 0.17 s vs 13.14 s (76x); headers 0.002 vs 0.044 s (22x); head 0.002 vs 0.023 s (12x); select 0.82 vs 19.27 s (24x); search 1.31 vs 25.63 s (20x); frequency 1.14 vs 29.17 s (26x); index 1.11 vs 14.22 s (13x); stats 12.97 vs 74.25 s (5.7x); sort 2.15 vs 47.58 s (22x); fmt 2.43 vs 37.26 s (15x). SIMD microbenchmark, ASM vs naive C at gcc -O2: scan_count_byte 8.9 vs 3.3 GB/s (2.7x), scan_find_byte 11.3 vs 2.3 GB/s (5.0x), scan_find_byte early hit 8 ns vs 88 ns (10.8x), parse_get_field ~20 ns vs ~50 ns (~2.5x).
corrections.workload: 1 GB CSV (6.27M rows, 18 columns, generated by test/gen.py with no quoted fields): count, headers, head, select, search, frequency, index, stats, sort, fmt, timed best-of-3 after one warmup; plus a 16 MB buffer byte-count/byte-find microbenchmark and a 160-byte field-extraction microbenchmark, assembly versus naive C. The shipped test/bench.sh actually generates and times a 500 MB file and has no fmt row, so the published 1 GB table is not what the script as written produces.
corrections.caveats: No CPU model (only 'Intel Core' under WSL2), no gcc version, no xsv version or build, no run-to-run spread. The xsv baseline ran far below xsv's own published throughput: 1 GiB in 13.14 s for count is about 82 MB/s and index about 75 MB/s, versus 413.76 MB/s and 379.28 MB/s in xsv's BENCHMARKS.md on an i7-6900K (derived from page data), which points at a slow WSL2 file path or build rather than parsing cost, so the 5.7-76x ratios are likely inflated. oxsv does less work by default: count only counts newline bytes, and quoted-field parsing is off unless --quote is given, whereas xsv always runs a full RFC 4180 parser; the generated test data has no quoted fields, so outputs agree here but would differ on CSV with quoted commas or newlines. search is exact match versus xsv's regex. oxsv memory-maps the file (an I/O strategy difference). The microbenchmark baseline is a naive byte loop at gcc -O2, not glibc memchr (itself AVX2) or an -O3 build, and its 'count' buffer has 1/256 newlines although the comment says ~6%. x86-64 Linux with AVX2 only. 0 stars, 6 commits over two days (2026-02-28 to 2026-03-01).

notes: Numbers match README and BENCHMARKS.md exactly; tier C stands. Shortcomings: CPU model and xsv version unstated, xsv baseline about 5x below xsv's own published throughput (derived), quote-unaware default parsing and newline-only count versus xsv's full CSV parser, exact-match versus regex search, naive-loop C baseline instead of memchr/-O3, shipped bench.sh times a 500 MB file not the published 1 GB one.

tier_reason: First-party README gives one Keil timing (10,000 bytes copied 10,000 times: rt_memcpy 1261 ms, assembly 883 ms, C library memcpy 906 ms); the repo holds only the three .S ports and SConscript, with no benchmark code, MCU, clock, Keil version or flags, so C.

corrections.caveats: Single undocumented Keil run: no benchmark code in the repo, no MCU, clock, Keil version, optimisation level or buffer alignment. The win over the Keil C library memcpy is about 2.6% (906 vs 883 ms, derived from page data), essentially parity; the 1.43x headline is against RT-Thread's own C rt_memcpy. The code is Silicon Labs uC/LIB assembly (Copyright 2004-2020 Silicon Laboratories, SPDX Apache-2.0 headers, ported to RT-Thread in 2020), and the README credits the LDMIA/STMIA load/store-multiple instructions (40 bytes per instruction pair), not assembly as such. Each call pushes R3-R12, which costs on short copies; buffers are not checked for overlap (memcpy semantics only). README is in Chinese. Last commit 2022-06-09.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly; tier C confirmed, metadata (Apache-2.0, 12 stars, 5 forks, last commit 2022-06-09, abandoned) checked. Split id: merged.json also holds https://github.com/mysterywolf/rt_memcpy_cm#asm-level-string-and-memory (confirmed C in batch-27); record one of the two as duplicate. Shortcomings: ~3% win over the C library memcpy, single unspecified Keil run with no harness, abandoned.

tier_reason: First-party hyperfine output in the README with a public bench.sh (hyperfine -i -N, odiff vs vxdiff on one pair), but no CPU, compiler flags, odiff version or image sizes, and the numbers predate later hot-path correctness fixes, so C.

corrections.baseline: odiff (dmtrKovalenko/odiff, version and build unstated), itself an already-catalogued project (wave 10)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Kernel assembled with nasm -g -f elf64 (meson.build); meson.build sets no optimisation flags and the justfile runs 'meson setup' without --buildtype, so the C front end and any subproject libspng default to meson's debug build; odiff build not stated
corrections.caveats: No license file (LICENSE, LICENSE.md and COPYING all 404; sidebar shows none), so the standalone repo is reference only; the same kernel now ships MIT-licensed inside odiff as src/vxdiff.asm, built by odiff's build.zig on x86-64 Linux and macOS. README numbers (README commits 2025-09-08 and 2025-10-03) predate hot-path fixes to the alpha/whitening code ('Fix computing masks for overwriting pixels with white' 2025-09-10; 'Fix transparent pixels whitening neighbouring pixels' and 'Remove redundant alpha=0 whitening' 2026-08-01), so the alpha row was measured on code later fixed. The bench is end to end (libspng PNG decode included) with no CPU, image sizes or odiff version; bench.sh uses hyperfine -i, which ignores non-zero exit codes, and one pair per run. The small-image result (15.10 +/- 29.81) has a standard deviation larger than the mean and the large-image gain (1.04 +/- 0.04) is within noise of 1x. vxdiff only counts differing pixels with odiff's default YIQ threshold 0.1; it writes no diff image and implements none of odiff's other options. Requires AVX-512.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly; tier C stands (metadata checked: no license, 24 stars, last commit 2026-08-01). Relation to a listed project: vxdiff's AVX-512 kernel was upstreamed into odiff (https://github.com/dmtrkovalenko/odiff, wave 10) as src/vxdiff.asm, nearly line for line; consider recording duplicate if the catalog treats upstreamed kernels like ports, otherwise keep with this note. Shortcomings: no license, end-to-end timing dominated by decode, noisy small-image row, numbers predate alpha-handling fixes, baseline version unstated.
